Case Information: A 65-year-old woman with no family history of endocrine tumors was referred to the General Surgery Unit. Over the past 18 months, she experienced increasing weakness, weight loss of up to 15 kg, angular cheilitis, and glossitis. She had a traumatic fracture of her left humeral head and underwent dual energy x-ray absorptiometry and laboratory investigations as an outpatient, which indicated severe osteoporosis (t-score −4 at the lumbar spine and −2.4 at the femoral neck), primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT), Hashimoto’s thyroiditis with hypothyroidism, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Recently, she developed widespread itching and painful rashes on the perioral skin, perineum, and groin folds. She was admitted to an Internal Medicine Unit for further assessment. Her father had died at age 84 due to myocardial infarction and her mother at age 69 after colorectal cancer surgery. A 60-year-old brother had arterial hypertension, and a 32-year-old daughter had severe obesity. Menarche occurred at 12 years of age and menopause at 39 years following hystero-adnexectomy for post-partum uterine rupture. There were no other significant medical history details, and she was not taking any medications. Biochemical studies showed iron-deficiency anemia and confirmed Hashimoto’s thyroiditis with mild hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, and mild pHPT (Calcium: 10.4 mg/dl [normal range 8.8-10.6], 24-hour urinary calcium excretion: 358 mg/dl [normal range 130–300], iPTH: 147 pg/ml [normal range 8–87], Creatinine: 0.74 mg/dl [normal range 0.84-1.25]). A 99mTc-sestamibi scan and ultrasound of the neck identified an inferior right hyperfunctioning parathyroid. A 9 mm nodule was detected by ultrasound in the left thyroid lobe. Endoscopic studies revealed mild antral gastritis and diverticulosis of the colon, while abdominal ultrasound showed no pathological findings. Skin culture indicated candidiasis secondary to Candida albicans with bacterial superinfection. The patient was discharged with prescriptions for oral antidiabetics, iron therapy, proton pump inhibitors, bisphosphonates, levothyroxine, and antifungal/antibiotic agents. After one month, with no improvement in the rash, she was referred to the Dermatology Unit, where a generic deficiency dermatitis was diagnosed based on histological examination of a skin biopsy. Oral zinc and vitamin supplements were added to her diet, but no improvement was observed over the following two months.
Diagnostic Tests: Abdominal enhanced multidetector-row computed tomography (MDCT) revealed a low-density 2x3 cm mass between the body and tail of the pancreas, with intense contrast enhancement. Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (OctreoScan) with SPECT acquisition showed an area of increased uptake between the body and tail of the pancreas corresponding to the tumor revealed by previous MDCT.

Case Information: A 76-year-old, right-handed, Caucasian female presented with significant gait impairment. She has a history of SS, evidenced by a decade of sicca symptoms, reduced tear production as shown by Schirmer's test, and the presence of anti-Ro/SS-A antibodies. Over the past 6 months, her gait rapidly worsened, leading to frequent falls and necessitating the use of a wheelchair for mobility outside her home.
Diagnostic Tests: There was urogenital dysfunction leading to multiple urinary tract infections, absence of tremor with bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity, a festinating gait with inability to take more than 10 steps without support, and upper-motor findings (ie, hyperreflexia and Babinski findings) without structural disease of the brain or spinal cord on MRI neuroimaging studies.

Case Information: The patient is a 13-year-old Japanese boy who was born at a normal weight of 2954 g. He presented with ectrodactyly in the right hand and left foot, along with syndactyly in both feet. Surgical correction was performed on the left foot at 1 year of age and on the right foot at 11 years of age, with no complications reported. Post-surgery, he is able to walk comfortably, and no further interventions are planned. Additionally, the patient exhibited dry skin and café au lait spots, as well as dental anomalies characterized by notched and narrower edges of the incisors, resulting in a peg-shaped appearance. There were no observations of cleft lip and palate, mammary gland hypoplasia, lachrymal duct atresia, or ankyloblepharon. The patient also has attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). There is no history of carcinomas in the patient or his parents.
Diagnostic Tests: The results showed no de novo, homozygous, and compound heterozygous mutations. Deleterious mutations (nonsynonymous, frameshift, or splice site mutations) with a frequency <0.5% in the general population of p63 that were transmitted from one of the parents were analyzed, and a maternally transmitted missense mutation (c.956G>A, p.(R319H), ENST00000264731) was found.

Case Information: An 8-year-old male from Cameroon presented at the Grace Community Health and Development Association outreach unit with progressive muscle contractures and weakness in the lower limbs, upper limbs, and trunk muscles over a period of 4 months. Initially, the weakness and contractures began in the lower limbs and within a month extended to the upper limbs and trunk muscles. This was characterized by flexural deformity of the elbow and ankle. The patient progressively experienced difficulty in walking or standing without support, poor head and waist control, and difficulty swallowing. There were no seizures, cognitive impairment, visual or auditory impairment, and no bladder or bowel dysfunction. A district hospital initially considered poliomyelitis, but stool samples tested negative for polio. His birth history was uneventful, with standing without support at 7 months and walking at 12 months. Other developmental milestones were normal, and he had normal motor and mental functions before the onset of symptoms. There was no history of measles, HIV, trauma, or hospitalization. He was fully vaccinated according to national guidelines. There was no family history of paralytic disease or mental impairment. Both parents are alive and well. On physical examination, the patient was conscious, afebrile, with no facial dimorphic features. Pupillary size and reflexes were normal. There was no ptosis or facial weakness. There was wasting of the upper limb, scapular, and spinal muscles, and contractures of the elbows and ankles. There was no calf hypertrophy or pseudohypertrophy. Muscle power was 4/5 in both upper and lower limbs. There was weakness in the cervical, lumbar, and pelvic muscles, evident by poor head control and swaying movements of the waist. Hypertonia was noted in the muscles of the arm and calf, with the upper limbs in a semi-flexed position. Sensitivity to touch, pain, temperature, vibration, and proprioception were preserved. Tendon and cutaneous reflexes were normal. He was unable to stand or walk without support. Gowers sign was absent. Cardiorespiratory examination revealed an irregularly irregular tachycardia with a heart rate of 122 beats per minute. There was no palpable abdominal mass or hepatosplenomegaly. The rest of the physical examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed a serum creatine kinase (CK) level of 350 IU/l, hemoglobin count of 13 g/dl, white blood cell count of 8700 cells/µl, and a normal metabolic profile.
Diagnostic Tests: Hemoxylin–eosin stain muscle biopsy analysis revealed non-specific variation of muscle fibres diameter. Atrial tachycardia was evident on electrocardiography (ECG).

Case Information: A 30-year-old male presented with a 7-day history of slow response and unsteady walking, as reported by his family. Clinical features included impaired calculation skills, limited language expression, unresponsiveness, difficulty climbing stairs, inability to walk in a straight line, and irritability. No other symptoms such as weakness, numbness, fever, cough, diarrhea, headache, nausea, vomiting, altered consciousness, or convulsions were observed. Skin manifestations, such as resembling staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome or a diffuse erythema with superficial erosions, desquamation, and cheilitis resembling acrodermatitis enteropathica, were not found in our patient. The patient had an unremarkable medical and developmental history, and his relatives did not exhibit similar symptoms. However, his scholastic performance was notably poor compared to his peers, having completed only the 8th grade. Neurological examination revealed delayed reaction times, impaired calculation ability, significant dysmetria on heel–knee–shin testing, and a positive Romberg test. Plasma total homocysteine was 296.90 μmol/L (normal value 0.0 ~ 15.0 μmol/L) and D-dimer was 9.38 ng/mL (normal value 0.0 ~ 0.55 ng/mL), both elevated. Auxiliary examinations, including blood routine, biochemistry, thyroid function, rheumatic immune-related antibodies, folic acid, vitamin B12 concentrations, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody examination, all yielded normal results. Neuropsychological examination results indicated a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 20, a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of 18, an International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS) score of 41, and a Barthel Index (BI) score of 55. MRI revealed cortical atrophy and symmetric hyperintensities in the bilateral lateral cerebellar hemispheres, primarily observed on DWI.
Diagnostic Tests: Whole-exome sequencing, followed by Sanger sequencing for verification, identified compound heterozygous variant in the MMACHC gene: c.609G > A (p.Trp203*), a nonsense variant inherited from the patient’s mother, and c.482G > A (p.Arg161Gln), a missense variant inherited from the patient’s father. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry-based blood amino acid and acylcarnitine spectroscopy demonstrated significantly elevated levels of propionylcarnitine (10.53 μmol/L, normal range: 0.30–5.00 μmol/L), the propionylcarnitine to acetylcarnitine ratio (0.50, normal range: 0.02–0.20), and the propionylcarnitine to methionine ratio (0.90, normal range: 0.02–0.30). Gas chromatography mass spectrometry-based urine organic acid analysis showed a significant increase in methylmalonic acid (76.9 nmol/L, reference value, 0.00–4.00 nmol/L).

Case Information: A 24-year-old African woman was admitted to the hospital for a femoral neck fracture following a fall on the stairs. Surgical fixation was planned. Preoperative evaluation did not determine the genetic type of her condition. She exhibited minor skin changes on her face and hands, with no history of tumor surgery. Neurological examination revealed a minor decline in intelligence quotient (IQ), an end tremor of the extremities, and an ataxic gait. She was calm, cooperative, and oriented in time and space, with normal muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes. Cardiovascular and pulmonary evaluations, as well as biological test results, were normal.
Diagnostic Tests: A preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan did not show any sign of brain abnormalities. The images did not show any lesions that could explain these symptoms.

Case Information: A 71-year-old female reported experiencing itchy lesions on the left side of her body that began 2 months prior. Upon physical examination, there were violet-colored, polygonal papules arranged along specific lines on the left side, including the left leg and arm. The patient has been on olanzapine for 2 years for schizophrenia. Examination of the mucous membranes and nails showed no abnormalities.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathological examination revealed orthokeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, lichenoid band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction, eosinophil infiltration, and dyskeratotic keratinocytes.

Case Information: A 70-year-old male presented with a single pinkish nodule located on the back of his right hand. The patient reported no symptoms such as itching or pain. His medical history includes long-term psoriasis, which has been treated with topical medications. He reported no family history of skin or hormonal disorders. Despite the lack of symptoms, the patient sought further information about his condition.
Diagnostic Tests: Blood tests showed no endocrine abnormalities including thyroid function. Histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen obtained from the nodule on the dorsum of his hand revealed orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis with patchy parakeratosis, prominent hypergranulosis, and diffuse dissecting mucinous deposition between collagen bundles, along with some bland-looking spindle cells throughout the dermis.

Case Information: A 59-year-old woman (patient no. 18196) presented with a history of progressive recession of the frontal hairline and loss of eyebrows since 2010. She had been intermittently treated with topical corticosteroids. Upon examination, after removing her wig, five bilateral, symmetrical rounded patches of alopecia were noted in the midline occipital, temporal, and retroauricular regions.
Diagnostic Tests: Dermoscopic examination revealed loss of follicular orifices with mild erythema and perifollicular scaling.

Case Information: The patient is a 9-year-old female child admitted to AVBR Hospital with an ear deformity and a short, deviated neck present since birth. She was born to parents who are not related by blood. The pregnancy was without complications, and there was no history of drug use or exposure to radiation. Her birth was uncomplicated, and there were no issues during or after delivery. She has developed normally. Her height is 119 cm, which is below the 3rd percentile for her age. On examination, her vital signs were stable. The right ear was malformed and lacked a visible vestibular canal, while the left ear had discharge. The neck was short and deviated to the right. There was kyphoscoliosis of the thoracic vertebrae. The right eye was smaller than the left and intermittently decreased in size involuntarily. Systemic examinations revealed abducens and right facial nerve palsy. An ophthalmic evaluation indicated retraction of the right eyeball.
Diagnostic Tests: Audiometry revealed profound hearing loss on right side and moderate sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. Brainstem evoked response audiometry was also suggestive of sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. Computed tomography (CT) spine showed fusion of the thoracic vertebrae, suggestive of Klippel–Feil deformity. CT paranasal sinuses were suggestive of the hypoplastic frontal sinus. CT brain was suggestive of right holesteatoma.

Case Information: A 32-year-old male farmer presented with recurrent swelling on the right side of the maxilla, persisting for six years. He had previously undergone surgery for a condition affecting the maxilla. The swelling extended through the skin and into the right nostril. Intraorally, the left maxilla was absent, and the teeth in the right maxilla were mobile, indicating involvement of the entire maxilla. Preoperative incisional biopsy results indicated a mixed type condition affecting the maxilla. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed no signs of metastasis. The patient underwent right hemi-maxillectomy with excision of the involved soft tissue after baseline investigations. The postoperative histopathology results were consistent with the preoperative findings. The entire specimen was sent for further histological examination.
Diagnostic Tests: The histopathology result showed a highly cellular tumor growing in nests with anastomosing cords and a papillary configuration comprising cells with round to slightly irregular nuclei, a coarse to vascular chromatin pattern, and prominent nucleoli. The cells exhibited peripheral palisading surrounded by stellate reticulum-like connective tissue in areas. Other areas showed highly atypical cells with markedly pleomorphic nuclei and abundant mitoses. The fibroconnective stroma had areas of necrosis. The resection margins were also involved.

Case Information: A 13-year-old boy was admitted in September 2018 due to severe respiratory distress and a global motor deficit, with the lower limbs more affected than the upper limbs. He exhibited motor regression, axial hypotonia with poor head control, muscle strength of 2–3/5 on the Medical Research Council’s scale (MRC) for the upper limbs, and 2/5 on the MRC scale for the lower limbs. There was generalized severe muscular atrophy and retractions of the elbow and knees, more pronounced in the distal segments. The patient was born from a non-consanguineous twin pregnancy at term without hypoxic events and has a healthy 19-year-old brother. In his first year, he was hypotonic with moderate motor delay, sitting after 1 year and walking without support after 2 years. He never achieved running, climbing stairs, or jumping on one foot, with the lower limbs consistently more affected than the upper limbs. At age 4, a neurological examination revealed a lack of deep tendon reflexes, tongue fasciculations, neurogenic changes on electromyography, motor deficit with the lower limbs more affected than the upper limbs, and muscular atrophy. A biopsy showed neurogenic changes. Genetic testing for 5q SMA was negative. Between ages 5 and 10, the condition progressed slowly, with severe proximal weakness, generalized muscle atrophy, swallowing dysfunction, ventilatory restriction, severe contractures, progressive scoliosis, and a lack of deep tendon reflexes. A gastrostomy was performed in 2019. After age 10, he became a wheelchair user, with significant motor regression. In March 2021, spine surgery was performed, after which muscular atrophy became extreme, and weakness was generalized. He lost head control and had limited active movements in the upper limbs. He exhibited paradoxical breathing without needing noninvasive ventilation or oxygen, had no deep tendon reflexes, and presented with dysphonia and a hoarse voice. There was retraction of the mandibular joint with limited mouth opening, subcutaneous nodules around the interphalangeal joints, with the upper limbs more affected than the lower limbs. He had no paroxysmal events such as myoclonus or seizures. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed frequent generalized slow waves lasting 1–2 seconds, rarely focalized, more on the left side, without clinical manifestations. Electroneurography (ENG) showed mildly reduced amplitude of Compound Motor Action Potential (CMAP) with an increased area due to reinnervation. Sensory Nerve Action Potential (SNAP) had normal amplitude and velocities. Electromyography (EMG) showed chronic denervation changes with very large, polyphasic motor unit potentials (MUP) and incomplete recruitment. An abdominal ultrasound showed no liver enlargement. Spinal X-ray revealed severe thoracic scoliosis (Cobb angle >100 degrees) with thoracic deformity and restrictive respiratory dysfunction.
Diagnostic Tests: Genetic testing identified three heterozygous mutations in the ASAH1 gene. The first identified mutation (NM_004315.5:c.458_459del) was a two-base pair deletion in position 458 of the coding region in exon 6 generating the substitution of tyrosine in position 153 of the protein to a stop codon – p.(Tyr153Ter), or p.(Tyr153*), leading to a premature stop codon and thus, to a truncated protein. The second identified mutation (NM_004315.5:c.1226T>C) was the T to C substitution of nucleotide 1226 of the coding region in exon 14, generating the substitution of isoleucine in position 409 of the protein to threonine – p.(Ile409Thr). The third identified mutation (NM_004315.5:c.35G>C) was the G to C substitution of nucleotide 35 of the coding region in exon 1, generating the substitution of arginine in position 12 of the protein to a stop codon – p.(Arg12Pro).

Case Information: A 5-year-old Iranian boy presented with speech difficulties, lack of concentration, walking disability at age 4 leading to quadriplegia, spontaneous laughing and crying, clumsiness, psychomotor delay, and vision deterioration at age 5. Brain MRI and EEG revealed bilateral white matter signal changes with preservation of white matter. No histopathological studies or skin biopsy were available. Urine organic acids were analyzed using GC-MS, showing a normal pattern with no evidence of metabolic disorders. There was no indication of tyrosinemia, glutaric aciduria, methylmalonic aciduria, Canavan disease, propionic aciduria, isovaleric aciduria, or other known organic acidurias in Iran. Neonatal screening, clinical chemistry, and metabolism assays were normal. The patient's parents are first cousins and have had three pregnancies: the first ended in spontaneous abortion before 4 weeks, the second is the male patient described, and the third is a 2-year-old girl who currently shows no signs or symptoms and appears normal.
Diagnostic Tests: We ended up with only two novel variants in MFSD8 and AFF2 genes. The c.325_339del (p.Val109_Ile113del) variant in the MFSD8 gene was a previously unreported variant and found to be homozygous in our patient whereas his parents were heterozygote carriers. It is a deletion of 15 base pairs (bp), which causes the loss of five residues. The c.259A>G (p.Asn87Asp) variant found in AFF2 was a hemizygous change in our patient; his mother was also heterozygous whereas his father was negative for this variant.

Case Information: A 67-year-old Indian male presented with an itchy rash on the lower back for 10 days. He also observed pigmented rashes in both axillae and the left inframammary area of his chest. He had no prior history of skin rash or drug allergies. His medical history included hypertension for the past eight years, managed with telmisartan. Three months prior, his ophthalmologist noted left head tilt associated with right eye hypertropia when his head was straightened. Eye examination revealed fatigable ptosis of both eyelids with a positive Cogan’s lid twitch sign. Single fiber electromyography indicated mild to moderate neuromuscular transmission defect without significant decremental response in repetitive nerve stimulation. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of his brain and orbits were normal. Computed tomography of his chest did not show any thymic mass. He was started on pyridostigmine, which led to improvement in ptosis and head tilt on follow-up. Dermatological examination showed a 5 cm x 5 cm hyperpigmented, purplish patch with an irregular border at the center of his back. Several hyperpigmented linear streaks were noted in both axillae. Two erythematous macules were observed on his chest at the left inframammary region. There were no skin lesions on sun-exposed or other flexural areas. Full blood count, and renal, liver, and thyroid function tests were normal. Screening for diabetes was normal. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C viral serology were negative.
Diagnostic Tests: Microscopically, the epidermis showed mild basal vacuolation with rare apoptotic keratinocytes. There was pigmentary incontinence and a mild superficial perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes.

Case Information: A 29-year-old female presented with recurrent episodes of slurred speech and right limb weakness lasting 1-3 hours, which began abruptly at 5 a.m. on the day prior to admission. These episodes occurred three times before progressing to persistent speech difficulties and complete paralysis of the right limbs by 1 p.m. on the day of admission. Brain computed tomography (CT) performed in the emergency department showed no abnormalities. The patient was transferred to the neurology department for further treatment. Past medical history includes a cesarean section under lumbar anesthesia 21 days prior to admission, resulting in the birth of a healthy baby girl. Seven years earlier, she experienced similar transient symptoms of slurred speech and right limb weakness approximately half a month after another cesarean section, which resolved completely. At that time, brain CT was normal, and no brain MRI was conducted. Family history includes the death of her mother over 10 years ago from an undetermined cause, a healthy father who declined further genetic investigations, and no siblings. Neurological examination revealed dysarthria, tongue deviation to the right, right upper and lower limb weakness with muscle strength MRC grade 1, absent deep tendon reflexes in all limbs, positive bilateral Babinski sign, bilateral pes cavus, no significant muscle atrophy, and sensory impairment. Routine hematological, biochemical, immunological, and thyroid function tests were normal, as were laboratory results for lactate, vitamin B12, and very long chain fatty acids. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after admission showed diffuse abnormal signals in the corpus callosum, posterior limbs of bilateral internal capsule, and centrum semiovale.
Diagnostic Tests: We confirmed a c.622G>A (p.Glu208Lys) mutation in the GJB1 gene.

Case Information: DM is a 5-year-old male who first visited the Yale-New Haven Pediatric Clinic between the ages of 2 and 3 years old with delayed gross motor milestones and difficulty getting into a standing position. There was no family history of neurologic, developmental, or muscle diseases, and no evidence of consanguinity. His pregnancy and birth history were normal. Physical examination revealed prominent calves and forearms, an awkward gait, and poor running ability. He arose from the floor in a slow, stiff manner, but without the classical Gower’s sign. He could jump, climb stairs, and get into a chair without difficulty. Muscle strength was good, tone was normal, reflexes were brisk, and flexor plantar responses were present. Sensation, fine motor skills, vision, hearing, and cranial nerves were intact. CK level was 175 (24-195). A muscle biopsy showed scattered areas of atrophic and hypotrophic fibers with a relative increase in endomysial connective tissue on H & E staining, and a predominance of type 2 fibers on ATPase staining. Hypotrophic fibers were either type 1 or type 2, with occasional hypertrophic/hypercontracted fibers being predominantly type 2. By the age of 4 years and 6 months, it was noted that he “gets stiffer after immobility but can walk it off.” Cold temperatures did not seem to affect these symptoms. Physical exam showed muscle prominence and grip myotonia followed by transient weakness. Eyelid myotonia was not clearly observed.
Diagnostic Tests: An EMG showed multiple runs of spontaneous positive wave discharges that varied in both frequency and amplitude and lasted approximately 2 to 5 seconds each. CLCN1 DNA sequencing showed a homozygous transversion in nucleotide position 936 (codon 312) of C to G, resulting in an amino acid change of serine to arginine.

Case Information: A 58-year-old woman presented in December 2018 with a mass in her right leg and a lesion in the right superficial lobe of the parotid gland. Initial fine needle aspiration of the parotid lesion indicated oncocytoma. Biopsy of the right leg mass revealed high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma, which was surgically removed, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. A chest CT scan was performed to check for metastasis, revealing multiple large bullae in the biapical, paraseptal, and bibasilar regions. The patient had no history of smoking, intravenous drug use, or family history of pulmonary disease. In 2020, the patient reported persistent pain from the parotid lesion, leading to a parotidectomy. Microscopic examination of the removed tissue showed a solid neoplasm with a thin capsule in most areas, with cells arranged in a sheeted pattern and interspersed with delicate vessels. The neoplastic cells had abundant pale granular to eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentric ovoid vesicular nuclei. The tumor morphology was consistent with the previous fine needle aspiration findings, where the tumor cells were negative for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF1), renal cell cancer (RCC) marker, and vimentin, but positive for pan-cytokeratin. Immunostains from the current tumor cells showed positivity for epithelial cell adhesion molecule BerEp4 and negativity for GATA binding protein 3 (GATA-3), tumor protein 63 (p63), and Paired box gene 8 (PAX8). The pathologic diagnosis was acinic cell carcinoma. The patient continued to be evaluated for cystic lung disease. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis was ruled out based on normal vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) levels, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency was excluded by normal AA genotype, and the autoimmune workup was negative.
Diagnostic Tests: A heterozygous c.117705_1177-3del intronic deletion in the FLCN gene was identified.

Case Information: A 4-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents and with normal developmental milestones, presented with drooping of both eyelids for 1 year. There was minimal fluctuation throughout the day, but symptoms worsened with exertion. Neurological examination revealed bilateral asymmetric ptosis and limited movement of the extraocular muscles, with minimal signs of fatigue upon exertion. Pupillary light reflex was normal. There was significant weakness in the finger extensors. Deep tendon reflexes were reduced. The remainder of the neurological examination was unremarkable. No skeletal deformities were observed, and there was no relevant family history. The neostigmine test was negative, and serum AChR antibodies were absent. Imaging showed no evidence of thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.
Diagnostic Tests: Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) test done from nasalis muscle at 3 Hz stimulation, showed a decremental response of about 15% in both area and amplitude. Two CMAPs were recorded from the median, ulnar, and the facial nerves after a single stimulus. The decremental response characteristically appeared first in the second CMAP rather than the first. No R-CMAP was recorded in the family members who were also tested.

Case Information: A 28-year-old female presented for a comprehensive eye examination in October 2019 at the Eye Clinic of the University of Campania L. Vanvitelli. She reported experiencing a gradual decrease in visual sharpness over the past few months. The patient has a history of myoclonic epilepsy accompanied by muscle weakness and significant motor impairment, which began around the age of 13.
Diagnostic Tests: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Sanger sequencing analysis of NEU1 gene disclosed an already described compound heterozygosity: Leu91Arg and Gly328Ser.

Case Information: A 46-year-old Caucasian female reported experiencing generalized hair loss over the past nine months, which had progressively worsened. She had no neurological or ophthalmological issues. Her medical history included Graves' disease and atrial fibrillation, with no record of inflammatory skin conditions. Surgical history included pacemaker placement, salivary gland excision, and Achilles tendon repair. Family history was non-contributory. She was a former smoker and consumed less than one alcoholic drink daily, with no illicit drug use. She had allergies to shellfish-derived foods but no known drug allergies. Current medications were venlafaxine, buprenorphine/naloxone, levothyroxine, metoprolol succinate, trazodone, and alprazolam. The review of systems was negative for weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue. On physical examination, the patient appeared healthy and was not in acute distress; vital signs were normal. Notable findings included prominent skin folds on the right and left superior parietal scalp, and right and left superior occipital scalp. There was also diffuse non-scarring hair loss on the posterior mid-parietal scalp and right superior occipital scalp.
Diagnostic Tests: One 6.0 mm punch biopsy of the right superior occipital scalp was obtained for hematoxylin and eosin stain, which showed subtle, non-scarring, non-inflammatory alopecia, representative of telogen effluvium. No features of a deposition disorder were identified; however, there is background intradermal melanocytic nevus with congenital features.
